blindSummary: This state/province operates religious criminal law as one of twelve jurisdictions where parallel religious courts have jurisdiction to try criminal cases. The religious penal code criminalises same-sex sexual acts between men and women for adherents of the locally dominant faith, extending beyond the federal statute's coverage; per a foreign government's country-of-origin note the maximum penalty for men's 'sodomy' is death across all twelve jurisdictions, with the statutory schemes differing in detail jurisdiction by jurisdiction. No trans-specific incident or documented morality-police enforcement appears for this state/province in the record. The parallel criminal jurisdiction exists on statute and is operational - the framework itself, not any recorded incident, is what a visitor encounters.
blindSourceSummaries: An international human-rights organisation's report (2004) on the extension of religious criminal law: the first jurisdiction in the bloc enacted its religious-law establishment statute on 27 October 1999 (in force 27 January 2000), and by 2002 twelve jurisdictions had adopted some form of religious criminal law into their legislation - to date the only ones where religious courts have jurisdiction to try criminal cases.
